pages.name: Up and across
pages.text: This is the transmitter from the last lesson, `S(p) = 0.16p + 4`, its current in mA against its reading in percent. From the [[input]] 25%, a beam rises to the line and turns across to read the [[output]], 8 mA, so `S(25) = 8 mA`. Drag the pointer to read other inputs.

pages.name: Read 75%
pages.task: Where does the beam from 75% land on the side axis?
pages.why: Straight up from 75% the beam meets the line, and straight across it reads 16 mA, so `S(75) = 16 mA`. The rule agrees, `0.16 × 75 + 4 = 16`.

pages.text: You can read backwards too. From 12 mA on the side axis, the beam goes across to the line and down to 50%. A pressure-difference cell sending 12 mA is indeed at 50% of its full pressure difference.

pages.name: Back from 18 mA
pages.task: The loop reads 18 mA. Which percentage sent it?
pages.why: Across from 18 mA the beam meets the line, and down from there it lands at 87.5%. Check it forwards, `0.16 × 87.5 + 4 = 14 + 4 = 18` mA.

pages.name: Two outputs
pages.text: This example pipe's rim, radius 5 cm, is drawn up against across, both in cm. From 3 cm across, the beam meets the rim twice, at 4 cm and −4 cm, since 3² + 4² = 5², so one input has two outputs and the circle is not a function. Checking with an upright line like this beam is called the [[vertical line test]].

pages.name: A price that jumps
pages.task: In this example tariff, a filled dot is included and a hollow dot is not. Is the price a function of the time of day?
pages.why: Every time has one price, 10p before 07:00 and 30p from 07:00. At 07:00 itself the filled dot counts, so it costs 30p.
